narrative: Your promotion was denied because the model estimated a 47.0% chance that you will leave the organization—nearly one in two. In this screening, that was treated as enough departure risk to withhold promotion. The strongest signal pushing toward leaving was that you have other job opportunities: among employees predicted to stay, only about a quarter had outside opportunities, while you do. The most stabilizing factor was your tenure in your current organization: six to ten years there pushed the prediction toward staying, and roughly one in three stayers share that tenure. Your overall experience of six to ten years, however, pushed in the opposite direction, increasing the leave signal—likely because broader experience can make outside moves more feasible. The combined picture is not that your performance is poor, but that the model sees an employee with outside options and portable experience, partly offset by current-job tenure. Next, you and the organization should address the retention concern directly. A career conversation should clarify what promotion path is realistic and what would change the decision. The organization should examine whether your pay, recognition and growth opportunities are competitive, since outside options are the strongest driver. You should also document your commitment and ask what specific evidence would show reduced leave risk, so the denial does not become a self-fulfilling signal.
